title: a year of service designed
hook: a graduation speech in an Upanishad tells students to treat the guest as a god

segments.voice: Yesterday, dana: the gift sorted three ways, and four questions: why, what back, when, to whom.
screen: `THE GIFT.` · `WHY, WHAT BACK, WHEN, TO WHOM.`

segments.voice: Students are about to leave their teacher's house. Their study is done. Before they go, the teacher gives them a last talk, the kind of advice you'd hope to hear at any graduation. Speak the truth. Follow dharma. Don't neglect your study. Don't neglect your duty to the gods and the ancestors. Then comes a run of short lines that some Hindus still know by heart. That farewell talk sits in the Taittiriya Upanishad, and one of its lines gives today's piece of a year of service: the people who come through your door.
screen: `THE STUDENTS ARE LEAVING.` → `THE TEACHER'S LAST TALK.` → `THE PEOPLE AT YOUR DOOR.`

segments.voice: The run of lines goes like this, in paraphrase. Let your mother be a god to you. Let your father be a god to you. Let your teacher be a god to you. Let your guest be a god to you. In Sanskrit that last one is atithi devo bhava. Atithi is the guest. Devo bhava, be as a god. Notice who's on that list. Mother, father, teacher: people you owe something to, people who came first. And then the guest, who may be a stranger, someone you owe nothing at all. The Upanishad puts them in the same row. The same talk goes on to giving: give with faith, not without faith, give with modesty, give with understanding. So the teacher sets hospitality and giving side by side, as a life's practice rather than a one-time act. In a year of service, this may be the piece closest to home. A spare chair at the table. The colleague nobody invites to lunch. The new family on the street. A cousin in town for a hospital stay who needs a place to sleep. The tradition doesn't ask for a grand gesture. It asks for a door that opens, and for the person who walks through it to be received with the care you'd give to something holy. That's a high bar. It's also service that can happen without leaving home.
screen: `MOTHER, FATHER, TEACHER, GUEST.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST AS A GOD.` · `HOSPITALITY AND GIVING, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `A DOOR THAT OPENS.` · then, large: `RECEIVE THEM AS HOLY.`

segments.voice: Picture your own front door, or the door of the room where you spend your days, and let one person come through it, someone likely to come by in the next few months: a neighbor, a coworker, a relative, a friend of your child. Notice how you'd usually greet them, then, without changing anything outward, let the greeting deepen inside, as if receiving someone who matters more than you knew. If you pray, you can see the one you pray to in that guest.
Atithi. The guest, the one the Upanishad says to receive as a god, let the guest be a god to you.
Your line: a name on your calendar. Tomorrow, the piece that keeps the rest alive. That's day nine hundred seventy-two.

screen: `DAY 972 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A YEAR OF SERVICE DESIGNED.`

howItsDone: Hospitality has a respected place in Hindu homes, and the Taittiriya Upanishad's line atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you, is a saying some families teach their children.
